Eggs of the Fiordland penguin (Eudyptes pachyrhynchus) incubate at a temperature of approximately 36 °C [T = 36 °C], and hatching occurs after an incubation period of about 35 days [ab = about 35 days]. This duration is consistent with that observed in other crested penguin species nesting in temperate rainforest environments. Chicks emerge weighing roughly 70 grams [Wwb = roughly 70 grams], a relatively modest birth mass given the species' considerable adult size. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings are brooded intensively by both parents, dependent on frequent provisioning to sustain rapid somatic growth. During the first few weeks of life, the chick's thermoregulatory capabilities are limited, necessitating constant parental warmth. The 36 °C [T = 36 °C] incubation temperature is critical for successful embryogenesis, and deviations from this thermal optimum can lead to reduced hatching success or developmental abnormalities. Field studies conducted along the southwestern coast of New Zealand's South Island have confirmed that incubation duties are shared equally between the male and female, with shifts typically lasting several days before a partner exchange occurs.

Nestlings enter a period of accelerated mass gain almost immediately after hatching, a trajectory that carries them toward the species' ultimate wet weight of approximately 4,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 4,000 grams] by the time they reach asymptotic adult size. This remarkable increase in body mass is fueled by frequent regurgitation of fish and cephalopod prey by both parents. The asymptotic weight of nesting individuals (4,000 grams) [Wwi = 4,000 grams] is comparable to that of other medium-sized Eudyptes species, reflecting a life-history strategy oriented toward building substantial lipid reserves. Under the thermal regime typical of an actively foraging adult (38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]), the fledglings achieve their first flight and nutritional independence at approximately 75 days after hatching [tx = approximately 75 days after hatching]. This fledging age is somewhat protracted compared to that of smaller penguin species, a delay that likely reflects the energetic demands of feather maturation and the accumulation of sufficient body condition for an independent marine existence. The downy chick gradually loses its juvenile plumage during this phase.

Puberty is attained at roughly 225 days after hatching [tp = roughly 225 days after hatching] under a body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], meaning that young birds become physiologically capable of breeding before their first year is complete. This relatively early onset of gonadal maturation is notable among seabirds, many of which delay maturity for several years. However, despite reaching sexual maturity at this age, individuals do not typically attempt to breed immediately. The time since birth at first brood is 5 years [tR = 5 years], indicating that first reproduction is deferred considerably beyond the point of puberty at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. This extended prereproductive period is common among long-lived seabirds and is thought to reflect the time required to acquire foraging skills, secure a breeding territory, and form a stable pair bond. The body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C] is consistently maintained during this period of adult development.

Once breeding commences, Fiordland penguins exhibit a slow reproductive rate typical of K-selected species. Females produce a clutch of 2 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 2 eggs per nest], although the first, smaller egg rarely survives. This unusual two-egg clutch represents an insurance strategy, with the larger second egg being the primary source of successful offspring. Only a single brood is attempted each year [F_R_i = single brood is attempted each year], constrained by the prolonged chick-rearing period and the seasonal availability of prey. The maximum lifetime reproductive output is therefore modest, a trade-off offset by high adult survival and a long reproductive lifespan. Under the thermal conditions of active metabolism (38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]), the maximum reproductive rate is achieved when females successfully fledge a single chick annually.

Maximum recorded longevity for the Fiordland penguin is 20 years [am = 20 years] at a body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], placing this species among the longer-lived members of the Eudyptes genus. This extended lifespan is consistent with a life-history strategy characterized by delayed reproduction, low annual fecundity, and high investment in each offspring. The oldest documented individuals have been recorded in long-term population monitoring studies on the remote islands of Fiordland, where banding returns have confirmed individuals surviving to two decades. This longevity, combined with the species' deferred first breeding at 5 years [tR = 5 years], results in a relatively short effective reproductive window of approximately 15 years at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. The consistent maintenance of a 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C] core body temperature underpins the physiological machinery that supports this extended lifespan. Senescence is gradual in this species, with older adults showing reduced foraging efficiency and lower reproductive success in their final years.
